newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian retail, building data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian retail, building data.

text.p: Australian retail trade rose by 1.1 percent in August, while building approvals were up 1.6 percent in the same month, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said.
Economists' forecasts had centred on a 1.2 percent fall in retail trade and a 1.0 percent rise in building approvals.
The retail trade data for July was downwardly revised from a 2.4 percent rise to a 1.0 percent rise. A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follows:
KAREN PRINGLE, TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"Even though we had been expecting a correction, I'm not entirely surprised that we got another rise in August. These figures have been very volatile, and to the extent that winter clearance sales boosted the July number, there was always the risk that they could boost the August number as well."

"The August number surprises on the upside, but you've had a substantial downward revision to the July number. As it is, it pushes down the year-on-year growth to 4.9 (percent), and the average for the last three months on a year ago is around about five percent, which in real terms is probably about 2.5 to three (percent). In my view it's still implying a deceleration in retail spending, and that's been going on for the last several quarters. I don't think it rules out at all a rate cut."
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"Even if we take into account the revision to the July number, we're still about one percent up over the two months (compared with expectations). Prices are under a lot of pressure, but volumes are still very strong. I haven't seen much anecdotal evidence of the clearance sales continuing through to August."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"Retail trade is still reasonably firm. There's a hint of a bit of strength running through. It could be just big discounting which is leading people to buy. Home building approvals also show a hint of strength. The implications are that economic activity is really on the boundary and starting to show some signs of improvement. That implies that the RBA is going to be cautious. I doubt whether anything is going to happen tomorrow morning. They'll probably delay it until they've seen the third quarter CPI and average weekly earnings which means early November before they'll make another rate cut."
MATTHEW DRENNAN, ECONOMIST, AXIOM FUNDS MANAGEMENT:

"The retail trade was much better than expected, looking at the strength we saw in July coming into August. The momentum is definitely slowing, but it's still ticking along at a better pace than the market expected. I have been looking at rates to hold flat and this ... will make the Reserve Bank (of Australia) a bit more cautious."
DAVID BASSANESE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"The immediate reaction to retail sales was that they were fairly strong, but now with July revised down, overall it's still a weak reading. A weak retail sales was expected at the moment. It's consistent with a rate cut still on the cards come November. (The rise in building approvals) certainly suggests the housing sector has turned the corner, is picking up."
